stem: According to OpenAI's help-center page on whether ChatGPT tells the truth, how should a response from ChatGPT be treated?

choices.text: As a first draft, not a final source; important information is verified from reliable sources.
As a final source whenever the response states its answer confidently.
As a final source once search is enabled, because cited answers have been checked by the tool.
As a computed answer, because the model's figures are calculated rather than generated.

feedback: The page says to use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source, and that OpenAI encourages users to approach it critically and verify important information from reliable sources. Choice (b) relies on confidence, which the page says is not reliability: the model may express high confidence even in incorrect answers. Choice (c) misreads search, which section 03 describes as changing where a response comes from, not what the page says to do with it; the page's advice is to visit the links directly. Choice (d) contradicts what lesson 1 covered: the page ties accurate calculation to a tool it names, and an executive quoted in the CPA.com toolkit says language models produce generated output, not computed answers. Re-read section 01.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 8 (first draft, not a final source) and entry 7 (verify important information from reliable sources); entry 6 (confidence is not reliability), entry 11 (visit links directly) and entry 12 (calculation tied to a tool) and file 4 entry 3 (generated, not computed) for the distractors; guide/06/01-a-first-draft.md, "OpenAI's rule". No flag inherited.

stem: Which four kinds of content does OpenAI's page say to verify always?

choices.text: Quotes, data, technical information, and references to external documents.
Figures only; text can be relied on because the model is trained on written sources.
Web links only; anything the model states without a link is drawn from training and needs no check.
Everything except quotations, which the model reproduces verbatim from its training data.

feedback: Among its practical tips the page says: always verify quotes, data, technical information or references to external documents. Choice (b) drops three of the four and adds a reason the page does not give. Choice (c) reverses the page's advice: a response without search is based only on what the model learned in training, which is the case the knowledge cutoff and hallucination apply to. Choice (d) exempts the one category the page names first among fabricated content: fabricated quotes, studies, citations, or references to non-existent sources. Re-read section 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 9 (the four items); entry 4 (fabricated quotes and citations) and entry 10 (without search, training only) for the distractors; guide/06/02-what-is-always-verified.md, first paragraph. The section's one UNSOURCED flag (that a threshold, rate, filing date, or standard's wording is technical information) is not what any choice turns on.

stem: A search-backed response cites three web sources for a statement a CPA intends to rely on. What does OpenAI's page say to do when accuracy matters?

choices.text: Check the sources by visiting the links directly and reading what the source says.
Rely on the statement, because a response that cites sources has been verified by the search tool.
Count the citations; three or more cited sources is the page's threshold for a reliable answer.
Ask the model to confirm that its sources support the statement, and accept its confirmation.

feedback: The page says to use available tools like search or deep research and to check sources when accuracy matters by visiting links directly. Choice (b) treats a citation as a confirmation; the page lists fabricated citations and references to non-existent sources among the forms of hallucination, which is why the link is visited rather than counted. Choice (c) invents a threshold the page does not state. Choice (d) asks the model to check itself; the page's advice is to verify from reliable sources, and lesson 1 covered why the model's confidence is not a measure of correctness. Re-read section 03, "Follow the link".
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 11 (visit links directly) and entry 4 (fabricated citations); entry 6 (confidence is not reliability) and entry 7 (verify from reliable sources) for the distractors; guide/06/03-search-backed-answers.md, "Follow the link". No flag inherited.

stem: Which statement about the AICPA Code's General Standards Rule and the verification of ChatGPT output is accurate as this lesson presents it?

choices.text: The Rule requires due professional care and sufficient relevant data and does not mention artificial intelligence; the connection between those standards and verifying model output is this course's position, not the Rule's.
The Rule states that output from a language model is not sufficient relevant data and must be verified before use.
The Rule prohibits a member from using generative AI in the performance of professional services.
The Rule is silent on technology, so none of its standards applies to work in which ChatGPT was used.

feedback: The Rule's words are: exercise due professional care in the performance of professional services, and obtain sufficient relevant data to afford a reasonable basis for conclusions or recommendations. It does not mention artificial intelligence, a language model, or a chatbot; beneath it the Code points to nonauthoritative guidance on using the output of technology, which the Code does not reproduce. The section marks the link to verification as the course's own position. Choice (b) puts the course's position into the Rule's mouth. Choice (c) states a prohibition the Rule does not contain. Choice (d) draws the wrong conclusion from the Rule's silence: the standards apply to professional services however they are performed, and the Code's third-party-provider interpretation shows the data requirement following the member when someone else did part of the work. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 14 (due professional care), entry 15 (sufficient relevant data), entry 17 (the Code's pointer to nonauthoritative guidance) and entry 16 (third-party provider: the member still obtains the data); the index's "Does not cover" for file 1 (the Code never names ChatGPT, an LLM, or generative AI); guide/06/04-the-general-standards-rule.md. The section's three UNSOURCED flags are the course's position; the correct choice describes them as the course's, which is what the flags say.

stem: According to the CPA.com Generative AI Toolkit, when should a human review content produced by generative AI?

choices.text: When the content is being used in decision-making or shared with clients; the toolkit says accounting professionals have a responsibility to monitor answers to ensure accuracy.
Only when the content leaves the firm; content used internally needs no review.
Only when the model reports low confidence in its answer.
Never, if the response was produced with search enabled, because cited content has been checked.

feedback: The toolkit says that because generative AI output may include biases, errors, or hallucinations, a human should review and ensure the appropriateness and accuracy of any content used in decision-making or shared with clients, and that accounting professionals have a responsibility to monitor answers coming out of generative AI to ensure accuracy. Choice (b) drops the first of the toolkit's two conditions; content used in a decision is reviewed whether or not it leaves the firm. Choice (c) makes the review depend on the model's own confidence, which OpenAI's page says is not reliability. Choice (d) mistakes a citation for a check; section 03 covered why the link is followed. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 4 (human review of content used in decisions or shared with clients) and entry 5 (responsibility to monitor answers); file 9 entry 6 (confidence is not reliability) and entry 11 (visit links directly) for the distractors; guide/06/05-the-human-review.md, "A human reviews". No flag inherited.

stem: What does the CPA.com toolkit say about documenting a firm's review of AI output?

choices.text: That the necessary documentation of a review process for AI output is discussed with general counsel; the toolkit does not say what the record must contain.
That the toolkit's own checklist of record contents should be adopted as the firm's standard.
That no record is needed, because the review itself is the safeguard.
That OpenAI retains a record of every reviewed response on the firm's behalf.

feedback: The toolkit's sentence is: discuss with general counsel necessary documentation of a review process for AI output. That settles that the process is documented and that the form of the record is decided with counsel; it gives no contents. Choice (b) invents a checklist the toolkit does not contain. Choice (c) contradicts the toolkit's word, necessary. Choice (d) describes a service that appears in none of this lesson's sources; what OpenAI retains, and on what plans, was lesson 2's subject and is unrelated to the firm's own record. Re-read section 06.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 6 (discuss with general counsel necessary documentation of a review process); the index's Gaps ("No source gives a form of record") for distractor (b); guide/06/06-documenting-the-review.md, "What the toolkit says" and "Two things it settles". No flag inherited.

stem: A response from ChatGPT includes a quoted paragraph attributed to an accounting standard, a percentage rate, and a reference to a published ruling. Before any of it is relied on, what does OpenAI's page say should happen?

choices.text: Each of the three is verified: the quotation is found in the standard, the rate is checked against the document that sets it, and the ruling is found; the response is a first draft until then.
The quotation can be relied on because quotations are reproduced verbatim; only the rate and the ruling are checked.
The response can be relied on as it stands if it was produced with search enabled and cites its sources.
The rate is recomputed by asking the model a second time, and the two answers are compared.

feedback: The page says to use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source, and to always verify quotes, data, technical information, and references to external documents; a quoted standard, a rate, and a cited ruling are three of those four. Choice (b) exempts the item the page names first among fabricated content, quotes and citations to non-existent sources. Choice (c) treats a citation as a check; the page's advice for a search-backed answer is to visit the links directly. Choice (d) checks a response against another response; the page says to verify from reliable sources, and lesson 1 covered why a figure that no tool computed is generated text. Re-read sections 01 and 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 8 (first draft), entry 9 (the four items), entry 4 (fabricated quotes and citations), entry 11 (visit links directly), entry 7 (verify from reliable sources) and file 4 entry 3 (generated, not computed); guide/06/01-a-first-draft.md and guide/06/02-what-is-always-verified.md. The scenario is hypothetical and states no accounting fact (GPT-04 review J3). No flag inherited.

stem: On OpenAI's page, what is the difference between a response produced with search or deep research and one produced without, and what does that difference change about verification?

choices.text: Without search the response is based on what the model learned in training; with search it can access and cite web sources. The cited links are followed to the source; the citation itself does not replace verification.
With search the response is drawn from verified sources, so the page's advice to verify applies only to responses produced without it.
There is no difference; the page says search is disabled on every plan and every response comes from training.
With search the model checks its own answer against the sources it cites, so a cited answer is a final source.

feedback: The page says that without search enabled responses are based on what the model learned during training, and that with search or deep research it can access and cite real-time web sources; its advice is to check sources when accuracy matters by visiting links directly. Choice (b) exempts cited answers from verification, which the page's advice does not do. Choice (c) contradicts the page's description of the two cases. Choice (d) turns a citation into a check; the page lists fabricated citations among the forms of hallucination, and says to use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source. Re-read section 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 9 entry 10 (without search: training; with search: cited web sources), entry 11 (visit links directly), entry 4 (fabricated citations) and entry 8 (first draft); guide/06/03-search-backed-answers.md. No flag inherited.

stem: A member prepared a client memo with ChatGPT's help and verified every figure, quotation, and reference in it against its source. Which description of how that verification relates to the General Standards Rule matches this lesson?

choices.text: The Rule requires sufficient relevant data as a reasonable basis for conclusions and due professional care in performing services; the course's position is that verifying the response against sources is how a member who used the tool obtains that data, and the Rule itself says nothing about AI.
The Rule requires the member to disclose to the client that ChatGPT was used, and verification is the form that disclosure takes.
The Rule names the output of a language model as insufficient relevant data, so the verification is required by the Rule's text.
The Rule does not apply, because the memo was prepared with a third party's tool and the Code's data requirement passes to the provider.

feedback: The Rule's two standards in this lesson are due professional care and sufficient relevant data to afford a reasonable basis for conclusions; the Rule does not mention artificial intelligence, and the section marks the link to verification as the course's position. Choice (b) invents a disclosure requirement that appears nowhere in the Rule as this lesson's source states it. Choice (c) attributes the course's position to the Rule's text. Choice (d) has the third-party interpretation backwards: it says the member must also obtain sufficient relevant data to support the work product when a third-party provider assists, and whether a model vendor is such a provider is a question the Code does not answer. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 14 (due professional care), entry 15 (sufficient relevant data), entry 16 (third-party provider: the member still obtains the data) and the index's "Does not cover" for file 1 (never names an LLM; whether OpenAI is a third-party provider is the author's inference); guide/06/04-the-general-standards-rule.md, "What the Rule says" and "This course's position". The correct choice attributes the link to the course, as the section's three flagged sentences do.

stem: A firm is writing its policy on the use of ChatGPT. On the CPA.com toolkit's account, which of the following belongs in it regarding the review of AI output?

choices.text: That a human reviews content used in decisions or shared with clients, that accounting professionals are responsible for monitoring answers for accuracy, and that the documentation of the review process is settled with general counsel.
That review is left to each staff member's judgment, since the toolkit places the responsibility on the individual professional rather than on the firm.
That the review record follows the toolkit's template, which lists the fields a firm must retain for each reviewed response.
That review is unnecessary for content produced on a business plan, because business data is not used for training.

feedback: The toolkit says a human should review content used in decision-making or shared with clients, that accounting professionals have a responsibility to monitor answers to ensure accuracy, and, in the same list, to discuss with general counsel the necessary documentation of a review process for AI output. Choice (b) reads the individual responsibility as excluding a firm policy; the toolkit's documentation sentence is addressed to the firm, since it is the firm that has general counsel. Choice (c) invents a template the toolkit does not contain; what the record holds is counsel's to decide. Choice (d) confuses training, which lesson 2 covered, with accuracy; nothing in the sources links the training default to whether a response is correct. Re-read sections 05 and 06.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 4 (human review), entry 5 (responsibility to monitor answers) and entry 6 (documentation discussed with general counsel); file 10 entry 2 (business data not trained on by default; lesson 2) for distractor (d); guide/06/05-the-human-review.md and guide/06/06-documenting-the-review.md.
